title: Returning Stack Addresses
concept: Never hand out the key to a room that will disappear when the function ends (a fatal bug)

The main frame is created and prepares to call `dangerousFunc`.

The key question is: "Is a local variable's address valid after the function returns?"

steps.title: Calling dangerousFunc
steps.explanation:
The call creates a new frame with local variable `x=100` inside it.

main's `p` will receive the pointer value returned by the function.

steps.title: Dangerous Return - Address of a Local Variable
steps.explanation:
`return &x;` returns the address of a local variable that is about to be destroyed.

After the function ends, that address becomes a dangling pointer with no valid target.

steps.title: Dereferencing a Dangling Pointer - Undefined Behavior
steps.explanation:
Reading `*p` at this point is Undefined Behavior.

The value might appear correct by chance, could be garbage, or might crash the program — it cannot be trusted.

quiz.question: What is the safe way to return data created inside a function?
options: Return the address of a local variable
Return the address of a static variable or malloc (dynamically allocated) memory
Just printf inside the function and be done
quiz.explanation: `static` variables are stored in the data segment, and `malloc` allocates in the heap — both persist after the function ends.

misconceptions.wrong: C doesn't give a compile error for return &x
misconceptions.correct: Most compilers only give a warning and let it pass.
misconceptions.why:
This is one of the most common mistakes beginners make.
Never ignore the warning: "Address of stack memory associated with local variable 'x' returned."

keyTakeaway: Never return the address of a local variable (&local) outside the function.
